extracted.intended_audience: educated eighteenth-century reading public (gentlemen, writers, educators, literate citizens)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative criteria and prescriptive advice from Spectator essays on epic poetry, education, conversation, and manners; includes standards for composing and judging heroic poems and for practical instruction in youth. Geared toward readers and practitioners concerned with literary quality and social conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_tradition_to_justify_fantastical_elements_in_epic
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should take the matters of fact as they came down in tradition and circumstance them to make them appear natural and agreeable; features that appear incredible may be justified if they are part of received tradition (e.g., the Harpy prophecy, the Trojan fleet changed into nymphs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Virgil preserves prophecies and prodigies found in the history of Æneas and qualifies or situates them (a prophecy voiced by a hungry Harpy, or a child's remark) so they are not ludicrous in an heroic poem; Virgil and Ovid sharing an element suggests its traditional authority. Where tradition records a strange incident, the poet may properly include it but should qualify or present it in a way that renders it suitable to the epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate_characterization_of_heroes_by_dominant_and_secondary_virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be painted according to the virtues that most distinguish them: e.g., Turnus is given Courage as his chief ornament (ostentatious, haughty language), while Æneas's Piety and other virtues out-shine his courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish types of valour—manifestation (ostentation, address) versus conduct and success; ensure that the hero's language, actions, and situations consistently reflect the primary virtues assigned by tradition or design so the character is coherent and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition_and_contravention_of_the_fable_as_principal_beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The disposition and contrivance of the fable (how incidents are arranged and how the story is contrived) is a principal beauty of an heroic book; fullness of incidents and natural progress toward events (as in Milton's ninth Book) are praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce a well-contrived series of incidents, with a clear and regular progression to major catastrophes; fill the poem with 'story' and incidents that make the book entertaining and give scope for invention while remaining coherent with the central narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal_authorial_intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; following Homer, fill every part of the work with manners and characters rather than authorial commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let characters, actions, and scenes convey meaning and moral reflection; avoid over-long authorial digressions that break the poem's dramatic immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_soliloquy_to_reveal_motive_and_character
rubrics_metrics.description: Soliloquy is an effective device to show an agent's restless purpose and interior motives (e.g., Satan's soliloquy introducing his second series of adventures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include well-crafted soliloquies where appropriate to expose inner deliberation, giving psychological depth and plausibility to actions without needing external exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural_and_apt_similes_and_imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Similes and images should be beautiful, natural, and apt; the closest and finest similes (e.g., the serpent rolling and the wandering fire simile) are of high poetic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer similes that arise naturally from the scene and deepen understanding or feeling; avoid forced or over-curious parallels. Frequent use of striking but fitting images increases poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicacy_in_moral_discourse_between_characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogues about moral questions should proceed from difference of judgment, not heat of passion; they should be managed with reason and delicacy (as Adam and Eve's dispute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose moral conversations to reveal character through calm reasoning and subtle sentiment rather than melodrama; this lends plausibility to virtuous persons and preserves dignity in sacred subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic_representation_of_nature's_sympathy_with_moral_events
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions that imagine Nature's sympathy (earth trembling, heaven flashing, nature sighing at the Fall) are poetically powerful and appropriate for divine or epic subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting cosmic moral events, employ grand, sympathetic natural signs to mark the significance of human actions—handled with imagination to avoid bathos and to reflect the moral weight of the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_classical_parallels_to_strengthen_and_guard_against_cavil
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing parallels with Homer or other classical authors both highlights beauties and guards the poet against critics ('by that means may be also guarded against the Cavils of the Tasteless or Ignorant').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wherever lines, incidents, or affects resemble established classical models, make that resemblance evident as an artistic choice or inheritance; parallels can be used defensively to pre-empt charges of impropriety or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education_tailored_to_purpose:_ornament_vs_use
rubrics_metrics.description: The design of learning is either to render a man an agreeable companion (study for ornament) or to furnish him with means to acquire an estate (study for use); most should be educated for use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a pupil's education aims at personal cultivation or practical advancement; for the majority, prioritize useful, practical instruction that will serve in life and business rather than pushing all toward high genius tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach_practical_skills_for_social_and_economic_advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical geometry, writing English letters, accounts, shorthand, and similar small accomplishments are of wide utility and can materially advance a man's fortune and social standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate exercises such as punctual reciprocal letter-writing (acting imaginary business roles), instruction in accounts, shorthand, and practical geometry; these skills are often more serviceable in life than classical studies alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_pushing_every_boy_to_works_of_genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammar schools' fault is pushing every boy to works of genius; many would be better served by acquiring modest practical arts which often lead to success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor curriculum to the student's natural talents—do not impose the same high-literary regimen on all; recognize that 'little Accomplishments' can open opportunities and that great genius has few suitable public posts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity_and_integrity_over_dissimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity is true wisdom: it is plainer, easier, safer, more secure, less entangling, and the shortest way to advantage; dissimulation soon fails and leaves perpetual suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate genuine goodness rather than merely seeming good; in business and conversation, be honest—truth creates confidence, saves enquiries, avoids the perpetual labor of maintaining false pretences, and has lasting returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_ostentatious_piety_that_makes_virtue_ridiculous
rubrics_metrics.description: Ostentatious displays of devotion (the Devotée) disparage true religion and make virtue ridiculous by unseasonable, indiscreet mentions of virtue and public theatricality in piety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious devotion should be sincere and proportioned to circumstances; avoid public posturing, exaggerated rites (praying oneself out of breath, ostentatious moralizing), or constant moralizing that deters others from true goodness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty_and_avoidance_of_affectation_in_manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty is tied to magnanimity and courage (Spartan modesty admired); affectation of smartness, bold looks, and boastful behavior are follies of urban youth and undermine genuine worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value modesty of countenance and behavior; discourage petty displays of arrogance or contrived smartness (tripping beggars, red breeches as mock valor). Modesty aids social respect and, in martial contexts, real courage.
